## 3.5. Magnetoelectric effect

First magnetoelectric measurements were carried out on a reoxidized slice of the phase-pure composite grown with 5 mm h 1 . As described in the experimental section, prior to the ME measurements an electric field of 5 kV cm 1 was applied. We would like to stress that without this poling step no considerable magnetoelectric voltage was measured. This proves that the electric field leads to a permanent electrical polarization and consequently the ferroelectric tetragonal modification of BaTiO3 has to be present although the c/a ratio is very small.

Materials that show coexistence of various functional 
properties have recently been attracting increasing 
attention due to the possible application in highly 
integrated multifunctional devices. Multiferroic ­BiFeO3 
(BFO) is one of such materials that shows both ferro-
electric (FE) and magnetic orders at room temperature 
(RT). BFO exhibits a high spontaneous polarization 
(~ 100 µC/cm2) with high FE Curie temperature (T) (TC
~ 830 °C) and zero net magnetization with a high anti-
ferromagnetic Néel temperature (TN ~ 340 °C). How-
ever, pure BFO suffers from high leakage and hence 
deteriorated ferroelectricity due to the volatilization 
of Bi during high-T sintering process [1]. The linear 
ME effect in BFO is forbidden due to the cycloidal spin 
structure [2]. In addition, the piezoelectricity in BFO 
is also very low due to the high leakage currents [3].

These samples show dense microstructures and distorted crystal structures, thus leading to high ferroelectricity with Pr ¼ 49 : 5 μ C/cm 2 , excellent piezoelectricity with d 33 ¼ 137 pC/N, improved magnetism Mr ¼ 0 : 47 emu/g, and high Curie temperature with T C ¼ 698 K in the x ¼ 0 : 8 ceramics, displaying potential applications in multiply controlled devices.

## II. MATERIALS AND METHODS

0.74BiFeO3 -0.26(Ba0 : 85Ca0 : 15)TiO3 -x wt. % MnO2 (BF -BCT -Mn -x ) ceramics were fabricated with a conventional solid state method using carbonate and metal oxides as powders: Bi2O3 (99.9%), Fe2O3 (99%), BaCO3 (99.95%), CaCO3(99.99%), TiO2 (99.8%), and MnO2 (99.9%). All the raw powders in the stoichiometric ratio of the BF -BCT -Mn -x ceramics were first mixed thoroughly in alcohol using zirconia balls for 15 h and then dried and calcined at 700 C for 2 h. The resulting mixture was ball-milled again for 15 h, mixed thoroughly with polyvinyl alcohol as a binder and then pressed into disk samples. After removal of the binder, the ceramics were sintered at 920 C for 3 h and then furnace cooled to room temperature.

In summary, multifunctional 0.74BiFeO3 -0.26(Ba0 : 85Ca0 : 15 ) TiO3 -x wt. % MnO2 solid solutions were fabricated with a conventional solid state reaction method. All the ceramics can be indexed with a coexistence of a rhombohedral (R3C) and a tetragonal (P4mm) lattice. The microstructure can be regulated by the addition of a small amount of MnO2. Large ferroelectric polarization values of Pr ¼ 49 : 5 μ C/cm 2 with a high Curie temperature of TC ¼ 698 K can be achieved because of the enhanced particle size and insulation. The improved remanent magnetization of Mr ¼ 0 : 59 emu/g can be understood in terms of the enhanced superexchange interaction between Fe 2 þ and Fe 3 þ arising from the increased Fe -O -Fe bond angle and the content of Fe 2 þ . Moreover, the x ¼ 1 : 2 sample exhibits the optimized piezoelectric coefficient with d 33 ¼ 137 pC/N arising from the relaxation regulation and the improvement of ferroelectric polarization. The coexistence of improved multiferroelectricity, piezoelectricity performance, and high service temperature indicates that the present materials may have potential applications in multiply controlled devices as promising multifunctional materials.

An  electrical  polarization  in  the  BiFeO 3   with  a  rhombohe­ dral R 3 c distortion of an elementary cell occurs as a result of an anti-phase rotation of the FeO 6  octahedra with a displacement of  cations  of  iron  and  bismuth  in  one  direction  and  anions of  oxygen  in  another  direction. [49] The  result  of  such  a  local breaking symmetry of the crystal is the appearance of the vector of electrical polarization P along the axis [111]. Applying external high-pressure enhances the deformation of octahedra, changes the angles and the lengths of metal-oxygen bonds, affects the structural properties, and leads to the emergence of new phase transformations. [50]
In the range of external high-pressure from 1.25 to 4.5 GPa for  the  BiFeO 3 ,  several  phase  transformations  associated  with the  appearance  and  coexistence  of  polar R 3 c rhombohedral (FE), nonpolar P nma orthorhombic (PE, GdFeO3-type), antipolar P bam orthorhombic antiferroelectric (AFE) (PbZrO3-type), and  nonpolar I bmm  orthorhombic  (PE,  nonstandard  setting  of www.advancedsciencenews.com I mma)  phases  occurs. [51] In  addition  to  the  polarization  vector P along  the  direction  [111]  in  the  FE R 3 c phase,  the  vector P along the direction in the AFE P bam  phase is added. [52]   During the coexistence of two different FE phases, a tremendous gain of piezoelectric properties occurs as a result of not only polari­ zation  rotation,  but  also  polarization  extension  near  the  mor­ photropic 'polar-antipolar' boundary. [53] Pressure-induced phase  transformations  in  the  Bi 0.9 La0.1 FeO3  will  occur  at  a lower ≈ 0.5  GPa  external  pressure  because  the  chemical  pres­ sure during replacing bismuth by 1 mol.% of lanthanum in the Bi1x La x FeO3 is approximately equivalent to applying 0.05 GPa hydrostatic  pressure  on  BiFeO 3 . [54]   In  the  BLFO-MZFO  com­ posite,  the  colossal  increase  in  polarization Δ P r / P r starts  at ≈ 1  GPa  (Figure  7b)  and  coincides  with  an  appearance  of  the pressure-induced AFE P bam  phase. [54]  Such a colossal growth of Δ P r / P r  is due to an additional contribution to polarization, both from the new AFE P bam  phase and from expanding the polari­ zation area near the border between the FE R 3 c rhombohedral and AFE P bam  orthorhombic phases. Additional contribution to pressure-induced growth of Δ P r / P r  can give pinning on interfa­ cial  'FE/AFE'  ( R 3 c / P bam ),  'FE/PE'  ( R 3 c / P nma, R 3 c / I bmm),  and 'AFE/PE' ( P bam / P nma, P bam / I bmm) boundaries. [7a]
Large  values  of  pressure-induced  relative  changes  in  the polarization Δ P r / P r for  the  new  composite  are  of  interest  and are  of  great  practical  importance  because  such  a  functional material  can  be  used  to  create  high-pressure  sensors.  The colossal values of Δ P r / P r = 11 200% at 5 GPa make it possible to use the BLFO-MZFO composite as a sensing element in ultra­ sensitive high-pressure sensors. For creating electronic devices to monitor high-pressure, where the presence of ME coupling in  the  sensitive  element  is  required,  it  is  advisable  to  use  the BLFO-MZFO composite HPT with Δ P r / P r = 1230%  at  5  GPa and with an almost linear dependence of Δ P r / P r on  the  pres­ sure in a wide range from 0 to 7 .5 GPa.

Fig. 4 depicts the temperature dependence of the dielectric constant ( ε ) and tangent loss ( tan δ ) of (BNFPT) x ceramics in the frequency range 1 kHz to 1 MHz for various x compositions. It has been observed that the dielectric constant increases with the in­ crease in temperature and Nd concentration [42,43]. This may be due to the fact that with a rise in temperature, the thermal energy increases the dielectric polarization. Similar behavior is observed in Dy-modified BFO-PTO [44]. However, dielectric anomalies at ap­ proximately 320 °C are seen at all frequencies and shift towards lower frequencies as Nd doping increases. In this work, the XRD analysis confirms the presence of two phases in composite (ferrite BFO and ferroelectric PTO phase), which has different electrical conductivity suggesting that the accretion of charges will occur at the phase boundary. An additional space charge polarization has been given to these charges, providing the Maxwell-Wagner re­ laxation phenomenon [45]. Also, a ferroelectric-paraelectric transi­ tion or abrupt changes in the tilt system and cation displacements can be blamed for the anomaly in the evolution of the dielectric, as reported by many researchers [44,45].

Additionally, it has been noted that the ferroelectric transition for undoped (1x )BFOx PTO correlates with the dielectric anomaly and occurs at 650 °C, dropping to 227 °C when lanthanum is substituted [46,47].
